howTo: Enter transmitted torque, solid-shaft diameter, free length, and shear modulus using the units shown by the calculator.
Add an allowable shear-stress value only when it is traceable to the material condition and the design method.
Read stress and twist together: a shaft can pass a simple stress check while still having unacceptable angular deflection.
formula: J = pi d^4 / 32 | tau_max = 16 T / (pi d^3) | theta = T L / (J G)

examples.title: 30 mm solid shaft transmitting 250 N m
examples.description: An original elastic-torsion example for a uniformly loaded solid circular shaft.
notes: The stress ratio is only an aid to interpretation; it is not a fatigue or combined-loading verification.
A keyway, shoulder, spline, or coupling can govern the real design before the plain-shaft section does.

examples.title: 40 mm solid shaft transmitting 120 N m
examples.description: A lower-torque comparison that illustrates the strong diameter effect in the d-cubed stress relationship.
notes: Compare twist against the driven equipment's positional and vibration requirements, not only stress capacity.

references.title: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design
references.note: Use the applicable edition and project design method for shaft and torsion verification.

references.title: Project material and component data
references.note: Confirm material condition, allowable stresses, fatigue factors, and connection geometry against project requirements.

commonMistakes: Using a hollow or stepped shaft with a formula intended for a solid uniform circular section.
Mixing N m, mm, GPa, and MPa without checking the internal unit conversion.
Ignoring stress concentrations from keyways, shoulders, splines, or cross holes.
assumptions: The model assumes a homogeneous, solid, circular shaft in the elastic range.
It does not include bending, axial load, notches, contact stresses, plasticity, or fatigue.
Final shaft sizing must be verified against the actual load spectrum, connection details, and applicable safety criteria.
